The video editor I built started zooming in and changing the screen on its own. I never told it to. That's when I realized, oh, this is better than me.

It didn't start that way. The first version was like Frankenstein. Static cards. Ugly.

Here's what changed:

1. I saved what I liked. Every time a creator did something cool, I asked, can we do that?

2. Each one became a tool. An animation, a demo, a split screen, a zoom.

3. The editor picks from that toolbox. It decides where to zoom and when to switch screens.

4. I still review every cut. If something looks off, I give feedback and it iterates.

It took months. The toolbox is really just my taste, written down.

someone put 9 hours of blender next to one opus 5.5 prompt and cleared $9,340 off the argument

6.2M views, 318,000 likes on 12,400 comments.

split screen, no audio. left side is a blender timelapse, 9 hours of topology on one chair. right side is a text box, one prompt into opus 5.5, a python script runs and the same chair builds itself in 40 seconds.

the script finishes at second 11 and the clip runs to second 34. so what holds anyone through the 23 seconds after the chair is already done?

-> the left timelapse never stops. it keeps running under a finished chair and the gap argues on its own.

-> the generated chair has one leg 2mm short. comments found it in 4 minutes and the thread wrote itself.

-> the prompt stays readable the whole 34 seconds. people pause to copy it, and a pause counts as watch time.

-> the manual side is a hand on a mouse. a hand is a person, and people defend a person.

-> no voiceover, no caption. silence reads as a test, not a pitch, so nobody scrolls off it.

it works on anything with a visible craft cost, a logo, a cad part, a 40-track mix, a hand-inked frame.

opus 5.5 writes the bpy, blender runs it headless, descript cuts the two panels into one, $45 a month for the parts that cost anything.

the 40 seconds got the likes, and the 2mm short leg is what got it sent.

We forced a client to upload the exact same YouTube thumbnail for 14 months straight

Same shirt, same calm face, same black background, same layout on 31 videos in a row

His median views jumped from 2,393 to 17,517 and his channel scaled from 8,000 to 47,900 subs (pulling ~$200k/mo organically)

Everyone who tries to sell an offer on YouTube makes the same dumb mistake: they design a brand-new, "creative" thumbnail for every single upload

When RP Profits came to us, he had 32 well-designed thumbnails that looked like they came from 32 different channels. A dark chart on Monday, a lifestyle split-screen on Wednesday, a shocked face with cash on Friday

If you make money from $4 AdSense RPMs, you can get away with that. If you make money selling a $2,000 to $10,000 offer, it kills you

Because nobody buys a high-ticket offer off 1 video. They buy after watching 4 of your videos, and they only click 4 of your videos if they instantly recognize your shape in their feed

Look at how crazy the split-test numbers were across 64 of his uploads:

• 16 months earlier, RP put the words "9:30 AM EVERYDAY" on a bright, colorful thumbnail with a shocked face. It got 2,887 views
• We put those EXACT same words onto our 6-part black thumbnail formula across 7 different videos. They averaged 25,031 views (nearly 9x higher for the exact same words)
• Across 64 videos total, the 31 formula thumbnails averaged 20,007 views. The 33 non-formula thumbnails averaged 4,501 views (4.4x difference)
• Halfway through, we got lazy for 4 months and posted 30 videos with yachts, beaches, and raw screenshots. Views crashed to 4,197. We dropped ONE formula thumbnail in the middle of that slump and it hit 12,356 views, beating 29 of the 30 videos around it

You don't need to be a trader to copy this in 20 minutes today:

1. Use a black or dark grey background so it pops against YouTube's bright feed
2. Put your "Buyer's Candlestick" on one side: NOT a Lambo, put the one screen or dashboard your buyer checks every single day (a Stripe graph if you sell to founders like Instantly. ai does, a calendar full of booked calls if you sell sales, a P&L if you sell finance)
3. Put your calm face in the exact same shirt on the other side (shocked faces scream clickbait, calm says "I actually do this")
4. Use 5 words max that add the feeling ("It's so f*cking simple") without repeating the title

bro Claude Code spent 512 seconds building a mechanical chameleon while Blender rendered the same scene in 14 

And somehow this gets even funnier when you compare all 3 rounds

→ Round 1: 128s vs 3.5s
→ Round 2: 497s vs 13.6s
→ Round 3: 512s vs 14s

That’s roughly 36x faster for Blender across all three comparisons

Obviously rendering and generating an entire 3D scene aren’t the same task

But watching an AI spend 8 minutes figuring out a robotic lizard while Blender finishes its render in seconds is genuinely hilarious
